prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Because there are avenues Of traffic lights, a phone book Of brothers and lawyers, Why should you think your purse Will not be tugged from your arm Or the screen door Will remain latched Against the man Who hugs and kisses His pillow In the corridor of loneliness? There is a window of light A sprinkler turning As the earth turns, And you do not think of the hills And of the splintered wrists it takes To give you The heat rising toward the ceiling. You expect your daughter To be at the door any moment And your husband to arrive With the night That is suddenly all around. You expect the stove to burst A collar of fire When you want it, The siamese cats To move against your legs, purring. But remember this: Because blood revolves from one lung to the next, Why think it will After tonight?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Why, Will

Here are three ways to polish the text, depending on your intended context:

### Option 1: Elegant & Evocative Prose (Recommended for speeches, essays, or narrative writing)
> Simply because traffic lights line the avenues and directories are filled with brothers and lawyers, why assume your purse will never be snatched from your arm, or that your screen door will remain securely latched against the lonely stranger who embraces his pillow in the hallway of isolation? You look upon a window of light and a sprinkler turning in harmony with the rotating earth, yet you give no thought to the distant hills, nor the broken, aching wrists required to yield the heat now rising toward your ceiling. You take for granted that your daughter will walk through the door at any moment, and that your husband will arrive alongside the night that has suddenly enveloped you. You expect the stove to ignite a ring of fire on command, and the Siamese cats to weave against your legs, purring. But remember this: merely because blood circulates from one lung to the next right now, what makes you assume it will continue to do so after tonight?

---

### Option 2: Sophisticated & Authoritative Style (More structured and formal)
> Just because our streets are orderly with traffic lights and our directories are populated with family and legal counsel, why should you believe yourself immune to misfortune? Why assume your purse cannot be torn from your grip, or that a simple screen door will shield you from a man consumed by profound isolation? We witness illuminated windows and garden sprinklers turning alongside the earth, rarely considering the remote landscapes and the grueling, physically taxing labor required to heat our homes. We live in constant anticipation of routine comforts—expecting a daughter’s imminent return, a husband’s arrival as night falls, the stove to yield a ring of flame at our command, and house pets to brush against our ankles, purring. Yet, consider this sobering truth: simply because your pulse flows predictably from one lung to the next in this moment, why assume it will continue after tonight?

Here is a complete rewrite of the passage, retaining all original facts and themes while using new phrasing and sentence structures:

Just because cities have regulated traffic signals and directories filled with legal aid or family members, why assume you are immune to having your handbag snatched, or that your screen door will successfully block an isolated, desperate person seeking comfort from entering? 

A lit window illuminates a lawn irrigator spinning in rhythm with the earth's rotation, yet you rarely consider the agonizing physical labor in the hills required to generate the warmth rising in your room. You take for granted that your child will walk through the door at any second, and that your spouse will return home as darkness falls around the house. You anticipate the gas burner igniting on demand and your purring felines rubbing against your legs. 

Keep this warning in mind, however: simply because your body successfully circulates oxygenated blood right now is no guarantee that your life will continue past this evening.
outputs.L3:
**The Thin Shield of Civilization: Reflections on Comfort, Order, and Fragility**

Humanity has spent millennia constructing institutions, routines, and physical comforts designed to ward off the chaos of the natural world. Within the boundaries of modern society, it is easy to adopt the belief that life is secure, predictable, and permanent. Yet, this feeling of absolute stability is largely an illusion—a delicate veneer supported by systems and labor we rarely see, and masking a fundamental vulnerability that defines the human condition.

This quiet complacency is most visible within the domestic sphere. Day after day, individuals sink into the warmth of their predictable routines, surrounding themselves with the safety and quiet affection of home. Within these comfortable spaces, people routinely enjoy an abundance of modern luxuries—climate-controlled rooms, instant electricity, and readily available food—without a thought for the reality of their creation. We consume these marvels while remaining largely blind to the unseen physical labor, grueling hardship, and dangerous toil required by workers around the globe to produce and maintain them. The warmth of a hearth or the convenience of a modern device is paid for by sweat and strain that modern consumers conveniently choose to forget.

Beyond the walls of the home, we place an equivalent faith in the architecture of modern civilization. We walk through public spaces assuming that modern legal systems, law enforcement, and social contracts act as an unbreakable force field around us. However, these institutions are mere abstractions. While they provide a framework for order, they offer no absolute guarantee of safety. They cannot physically block a crime, nor can they fully insulate a community from the sudden, unpredictable intrusions of desperate individuals driven past the brink by poverty, mental illness, or hardship. The law can punish after the fact, but it cannot guarantee immunity in the moment.

Ultimately, these domestic blinds and social illusions mask a deeper, inescapable truth: human existence is inherently fragile. Beneath our complex legal codes, our hidden supply chains, and our cherished daily routines lies a delicate biological reality. There is no cosmic assurance that the heart will continue to beat, that the lungs will draw the next breath, or that the essential biological and environmental processes sustaining us will endure beyond the present second. To live is to exist on a knife’s edge. 

Recognizing this reality is not an invitation to despair, but a call to awareness. By confronting the hidden labor that sustains our comfort, the limitations of our social protections, and the sheer precariousness of life itself, we are forced out of our complacency. Only then can we truly appreciate the fleeting warmth of the present moment and treat our fragile world—and each other—with the care it desperately requires.
outputs.L4:
**The Thin Veneer of Sanctuary: Domestic Illusion and Existential Fragility**

Within the quiet confines of the modern home, we build a world designed to keep chaos at bay. We draw the curtains, lock the heavy wooden doors, adjust the thermostat to a pleasant warmth, and settle into the reassuring rhythm of daily routine. The gentle hum of refrigerators, the glow of ambient lighting, and the predictable schedule of work and leisure lull us into a profound sense of security. We convince ourselves that these walls do not merely shelter us from the weather, but shield us from the precarious nature of the world outside. However, this sense of permanent order is a carefully constructed fiction—an illusion that a closer examination of our domestic sanctuary quickly dispels.

To truly understand the nature of our modern comfort, one must first look at the invisible machinery that sustains it. The ease of contemporary domestic life does not exist in a vacuum; it is continuously manufactured by a vast, hidden network of human labor. The warmth of a heated room, the abundance of food in the pantry, and the instant convenience of clean water are all subsidized by unseen hands. Somewhere beyond our line of sight, men and women labor in fields, factory floors, shipping yards, and power plants—often in grueling conditions—to maintain the infrastructure of our peace. Our tranquility relies entirely on a complex web of human effort that we routinely forget or choose to ignore, enjoying the fruits of labor while remaining detached from the human cost that makes our leisure possible.

Yet, even if the supply chains hold and the unseen labor continues uninterrupted, the safety we construct within our four walls remains entirely permeable to danger. The poem reminds us that the threats to human life are not halted by a deadbolt or an alarm system. Inescapable dangers lurk just beneath the surface of the mundane. A microscopic virus, a sudden shift in political or environmental stability, a electrical spark behind the drywall, or a singular moment of tragic chance can shatter the peaceful atmosphere of a home in an instant. The universe operates on laws indifferent to our comfort, and no amount of technology or preparation can fully insulate us from the inherent risks of being alive.

Ultimately, this contrast between interior peace and exterior reality exposes the profound fragility of human privilege and existence itself. Privilege may grant us the ability to buy a temporary respite from the harsher elements of the world, but it cannot purchase true immunity. The sense that we are entitled to a smooth, uninterrupted tomorrow is a luxury of the comfortable, yet it is as delicate as spun glass. 

In laying bare these hidden truths, the poem serves as a stark, necessary awakening. It dismantles the hypnotic trance of daily routines and challenges our complacent assumption of permanence. By reminding us that the structures holding our lives together are fragile and provisional, it forces a confrontation with our own mortality and vulnerability. Neither our cherished comforts, nor our tightly managed schedules, nor life itself are guaranteed to continue into the next hour. To recognize this is not to descend into despair, but to shed our ignorance—to see our lives clearly, recognizing that every quiet, unburdened moment is not a permanent right, but a fleeting and miraculous exception to the chaos of the world.
outputs.L5:
Throughout history, humanity's greatest leaps forward have always begun with a single, profound question: **Why**? It is the spark of curiosity that drives us to look beyond the horizon, to challenge the status quo, and to seek meaning in an ever-changing world. Without asking why, we remain stationary, accepting existence as it is rather than imagining what it could become. 

Yet, asking the question is only the first step; finding the answer provides us with our ultimate drive. We push through adversity and embrace difficult challenges **because** we harbor a deep desire to learn, to grow, and to create a meaningful legacy. This underlying reason acts as our anchor during times of uncertainty, reminding us that our struggles are not in vain, but are instead the essential steps required to build something lasting.

Ultimately, when curiosity meets purpose, a powerful transformation occurs. Understanding our reason for being fuels our determination and clears the path ahead. Guided by this clarity and conviction, we **will** continue to overcome obstacles, push boundaries, and shape a brighter future for generations to come.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, reflective poem about how the comfort and predictability of domestic routines lull us into a false sense of security about our own mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
We measure mornings out in level spoons,
The kettle hums its dull, domestic grace.
We do not look for specters in the rooms,
Nor see the shadow lengthening on the glass.

The deadbolt turns with heavy, polished steel—
A foolish oath against the waiting dark.
We smooth the quilt, we sit to eat a meal,
And trace the table’s smooth, familiar mark.

How comforting, the choreograph of home:
The folded towels, the sweeping of the floor.
We build a castle out of dust and foam,
And think we’ve barred the stranger at the door.

We set the small alarm for seven AM,
A quiet arrogance that claims the sun,
Chanting the mundane like a sacred hymn,
As if our threads could never be unspun.

Wrapped in the warmth of laundered, fragrant thread,
We drown the terror of our fleeting breath.
It is not darkness that prepares the bed,
But soft habit that disguises death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a contemporary free-verse poem in the style of Stephen Dunn that uses vivid everyday imagery—like city streets, a home radiator, and purring cats—to build up to a chilling reminder that life can end at any moment.
counterfactuals.output:
The city at six o’clock was mostly exhaust  
and damp wool, the streetlights coming on  
with that faint, hummed hesitation  
before settling into yellow.  
On Fourth, a taxi slid through the slush,  
tail lights bleeding red into the dark,  
and I paused at the curb simply because the sign  
told me to wait, though the street was empty,  
as if obedience could keep us safe.  

Upstairs, the radiator was playing its usual music,  
that iron clatter and hiss,  
filling the room with the dry, familiar dust of winter.  
I took off my coat. The cat came over,  
stepping carefully across the floorboards,  
then collapsed into my lap like a sack of warm flour,  
her purr a low motor running on nothing but grace.  

How easily we are lulled by the domestic.  
The tea kettle cools on the stove;  
the book on the armrest remains open  
to the chapter where nothing bad has happened yet.  
We trust the floor to hold.  
We trust the quiet to mean that the world  
has agreed to leave us alone for the evening.  

And then, without warning, the rhythm shifts—  
not in the room, but in the thought of the room.  
You remember the driver who looked down at his phone,  
the stray clot wandering the dark corridors of a vein,  
the precise, indifferent math of an icy turn.  
The cat blinks, heavy-lidded, content in her skin.  
She doesn’t know that the radiator will go on knocking,  
stubborn and warm, long after the chest stops rising,  
or that the room requires so little of us  
to go on being a room without us in it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressing the reader directly ("you"), questioning why they expect their cozy evening routine and family to always be safe despite the quiet dangers and fragility of existence.
counterfactuals.output:
You turn the deadbolt, click the lamp,
and watch the kettle breathe its steam.
The hallway loses winter’s damp;
your children drift into a dream.
You smooth the blanket, stack the plate,
and sip your tea in quiet grace,
convinced that nothing dark or great
could ever breach this shielded place.

Who promised you the roof would hold?
Who signed the deed that bought you peace?
You trade the shadows for the gold
of simple routines that never cease—
the bedtime story, the folded cloth,
the whisper of a steady breath.
You live as if you were not the moth,
as if the glass were proof 'gainst death.

What makes you trust the floorboards beneath your feet?
What makes you sure tomorrow arrives on time?
A straying cell, a silent street,
a sudden, quiet, faultless crime
of gravity, or time, or chance—
it takes so little to erase
the gentle, domestic, daily dance
you take for granted in this space.

It is not that horror waits outside,
or monsters linger at the pane;
it’s just how thin the walls abide
between the shelter and the rain.
A universe indifferent, vast,
is balancing a quiet thread.
How do you sleep, convinced it lasts—
the warm roof hanging o'er your head?

Go on, then. Kiss them where they lie.
Check on the stove, turn off the light.
Hold tight to what you measure by,
and wrap yourself against the night.
Enjoy the warmth. Rest if you can.
But know the dark is wide and deep,
and safety is a fleeting plan
you only believe in when you sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a modern poem about the illusion of safety in middle-class life, contrasting items of daily comfort (a stove, a lawn sprinkler, phone books) with the underlying loneliness and violence of the world.
counterfactuals.output:
The arc-sprinkler beats its metallic rhythm—
*ch-ch-ch-tssss*—a mechanical, domesticated rain
sweeping over fescue kept precisely three inches high.
It waters the perimeter, the paved boundary,
a ritual to prove that even weather can be bought 
and set to a timer.

Inside, the induction stove glows a tame, controlled red.
Fire, stripped of its smoke and wild appetite,
simmers a stew beneath a glass lid.
We stand at the granite island, counting calories,
measuring water, convincing ourselves that danger
is something that only happens to people
who forget to double-lock their doors.

Under the pantry shelf, two heavy phone books from a decade ago
sit like yellowed sandbags against an encroaching tide.
Thick directories of names, numbers, addresses—
a paper illusion that we were once a neighborhood,
that we belonged to a city that could be indexed and bound.
Now they just collect dust beneath the paper towels,
as we sit in the blue light of our handheld glass,
scrolling past catastrophes in thirty-second clips,
eating dinner alone in a house full of people.

The walls are three-eighths-inch drywall and hollow wood,
yet we trust them to hold back the dark.
We hear the distant siren on the highway and turn up the TV.
We read about the war across the sea, the shriek in the alley,
the sudden, senseless rupture of a Tuesday afternoon,
and we adjust the thermostat by two degrees.

We are so safe here, surrounded by warranties and smoke detectors.
So safe, as the quiet in the hallway grows heavy as lead.
So safe, as the terror of the world presses its dark, wet face
right up against the double-paned glass,
watching us stir the pot,
waiting for the power to go out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short contemporary poem about not taking tomorrow for granted.
counterfactuals.output:
We fold our lives into next week’s pocket,
saving the good wine, the long phone call,
the quiet *I love you* for an evening
we assume is guaranteed.

We treat the morning like a subscription,
auto-renewed, unending.
We leave the best parts on pause,
waiting for a better time to play them.

But the calendar is not a contract,
and Tuesday holds no promises.

So drink the steam above your coffee now.
Forgive the mess, kiss the warm cheek.
Step fully into this unrepeatable light—
because this breath is the only one
currently holding your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
